title: Corsica
dek: Two women at Tomino in Cap Corse, and the reason this archive expects them to be strangers.
lead:
This archive holds **two people in Corsica**, and has never read a record for either. They are **Cattarina Defranceschi** and **Marie Jerome Defranceschi, born Bastiani**, both of **Tomino** in the Cap Corse, and both reached this project through the family tree rather than through a register.

Until today the site filed Corsica under *«not ours»*. That was **a guess wearing the clothes of a finding**, and it is corrected here. The honest position is stronger and more interesting than either a connection or a dismissal.

why.heading: Why this is a parallel and not a branch
why.text:
The surname is Italian. It is Italian in Istria and it is Italian in Corsica, and **that is the whole of what the two places have in common** — which is to say, nothing genealogical at all.

What they do share is a **shape**. Corsica was **Genoese** for four centuries. Genoa ceded it to France by the Treaty of Versailles in **May 1768**, and French control followed the fighting at **Ponte Novu in May 1769** — Napoleon was born at Ajaccio three months later, into a family that had been Italian subjects the year before. **Cap Corse**, the long northern finger where Tomino sits, was the most Genoese part of the island: it looked across at Liguria and Tuscany, traded wine and men with them, and its surnames are Ligurian and Tuscan.

So a *de Franceschi* at Tomino is almost certainly **an Italian family that became French by conquest** — exactly as a *De Franceschi* at Vodnjan became Austrian and then Croatian by treaty. **The same surname, caught by two different empires, four hundred miles apart.**

That is a real thing to write about, and it requires **no relationship whatsoever**. This archive expects these people to be strangers, and will say so unless a register says otherwise.

hold.close: **Zero records.** Not one search had ever been run in a French archive for this surname, by this project, in any commune — and as of today the reason is clear: **there is nothing to search.** The Corsican material is the least-worked ground the archive has. It is also the ground with the **best access**, and now with a **route through it**.

route.heading: The archive is open, and it does not have a search box
route.text:
The Corsican records are at **archives.isula.corsica**, the Archives of the Collectivité de Corse — Genoa's old island under one roof, both departments together. It is free, it needs no account, and **it is not FamilySearch**, which is why this work could be done today at all. Its shell refuses a plain command-line client; a browser goes straight in.

Then the wall. **There is no surname field anywhere in it.** Every module — *État civil*, *Corsica christiana*, *Recensements de population*, *Registres matricules* — takes the same three criteria: **a commune, a date range, and a record type**. Ask it for a name and it answers, in so many words, that this is *une recherche non indexée*: an unindexed search.

So Corsica is the **same shape of work as Vodnjan** — images to be read, not an index to be queried — with three differences that all favour it. The records are **free and unblocked**. The commune is **tiny**. And there is a lever the Istrian books do not have.

plan.heading: How this archive intends to work it
rows: **The tables décennales for Tomino, all eleven decades, 1793–1902.** Alphabetical: read the *D* and *F* entries — **Defranceschi**, **De Franceschi**, **Franceschi** — and take every hit. This is the whole commune, cheaply.

**Then the same tables for the five communes around it** — **Rogliano, Ersa, Centuri, Morsiglia, Barrettali**. A Cap Corse surname sits in a cluster of villages, never one. All six are on the platform.
**Then pull only the acts the tables point at**, by commune, year and type. Full transcription, the archive's usual schema — and by then the reading is a known, small quantity.

**Then Corsica christiana, the pre-1793 parish registers.** No decennial tables there, so this is the expensive part — and it is where a Ligurian or Tuscan origin would actually be settled, which is the only place a real comparison with the Istrian story could be made.

**Prove nothing.** Every Corsican person entered gets the line **corsica**, and the page keeps saying *parallel, not branch* until a document says otherwise. The two women stay marked **tree, unverified** until a register names them.

open.heading: What is open
rows: Whether Tomino's registers survive for the early years

The online *état civil* is chiefly the **greffe** duplicate, and it is thin for the revolutionary years — most communes effectively begin around **year XI**, that is 1802–03. **Tomino has not yet been checked.** If its first decade is missing, the tables décennales will say so faster than the registers will.
Whether Tomino is one family or several
Two women of the surname in one tiny commune may be a household or a coincidence. **Nothing yet says which.**
Where the Corsican Franceschi came from
Liguria and Tuscany are the obvious candidates, and Cap Corse's whole history points that way — but *obvious* is not *documented*, and this archive has been wrong about obvious before.
Whether the Napoleonic officers belong here at all
Our own Namesakes page carries two Frenchmen of the name. They are recorded because they exist, **not because they are relatives**, and that has not changed.
Switzerland and Savoie, still untouched

Four **DeFranceschi** graves at Giubiasco in **Ticino**, and one **Pierre Defranceschi** at Gaillard in **Haute-Savoie**, which is effectively a suburb of Geneva. Both look like modern Italian labour migration and neither has been searched. **They are two more separate stories, not part of this one.**

source: People from the family's MyHeritage tree and from gravestone records; not one has been confirmed against a register. Historical background: the Treaty of Versailles of 15 May 1768, Ponte Novu, May 1769, and the Genoese administration of Cap Corse. Record availability from the Archives départementales de la Haute-Corse, whose civil registration for 1793–1902 was digitised in 2008–2009 and published for all communes.

lever.heading: The tables décennales, which change the arithmetic entirely
lever.text:
Among the record types the platform offers, beside *naissances*, *mariages*, *décès*, *baptêmes* and *sépultures*, is one that is not a register at all: **TABLE DÉCENNALE**.

French civil registration compiled, **every ten years and for every commune, an alphabetical index** of the births, marriages and deaths of that decade. They exist for the whole run **1793 to 1902** — about **eleven tables per commune** — and they are alphabetical, so a reader looking for one surname reads **one column of one page** per table rather than every act of ten years.

That is the difference between reading a commune and skimming it. For the six Cap Corse communes named below it is on the order of **sixty-six index pages**, most of which can be dismissed in seconds, against thousands of acts read line by line.

**The plan below is built on that, and it is the reason Corsica can be finished when Vodnjan cannot.** Vodnjan's Habsburg registers have no equivalent: an Austrian *Liber Defunctorum* was never indexed by anybody, which is precisely why the death register has to be read image by image.
